title: First introductions
goal: Greeting people, giving your name and surname, saying where you're from and what you do, and asking yes/no questions three ways — all with a single verb: 係.
bekal: greet and say goodbye like a real Hongkonger
give your name with 叫 and your surname with 姓
ask questions with 係唔係, with 呀, and with 咩

dialogs.title: 對話 1 — Meeting in class
dialogs.intro: Andi, a teacher from Jakarta, meets Wong Lai on his first day in Hong Kong. Notice that the whole conversation runs on just one verb.

lines.speaker: 黃麗:
lines.text: [你好|Nei5 hou2]！
lines.id: Hello!
lines.literal: you — good.

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.text: [你好|Nei5 hou2]！[我叫|Ngo5 giu3][安迪|On1 dik1]。
lines.id: Hello! My name is Andi.
lines.literal: you — good. I — be-called — Andi.

lines.speaker: 黃麗:
lines.text: [我姓|Ngo5 sing3][黃|Wong4]，[叫|giu3][黃麗|Wong4 Lai6]。
lines.id: My surname is Wong; my name is Wong Lai.
lines.literal: I — be-surnamed — Wong, be-called — Wong Lai.

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.text: [好開心|Hou2 hoi1 sam1][認識你|jing6 sik1 nei5]。
lines.id: Nice to meet you.
lines.literal: filler — happy — know — you.

lines.speaker: 黃麗:
lines.text: [我都係|Ngo5 dou1 hai6]。[你係|Nei5 hai6][邊度人|bin1 dou6 jan4][呀|aa3]？
lines.id: Me too. Where are you from?
lines.literal: I — also — am. you — are — which — place — person — huh.

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.text: [我係|Ngo5 hai6][印尼人|Jan3 nei4 jan4]。[你呢|Nei5 ne1]？
lines.id: I'm Indonesian. And you?
lines.literal: I — am — Indonesia — person. you — how-about.

lines.speaker: 黃麗:
lines.text: [我係|Ngo5 hai6][香港人|Hoeng1 gong2 jan4]。[你|Nei5][係唔係|hai6 m4 hai6][學生|hok6 saang1][呀|aa3]？
lines.id: I'm from Hong Kong. Are you a student?
lines.literal: I — am — Hong-Kong — person. you — are — not — are — student — huh.

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.text: [唔係|M4 hai6]，[我係|ngo5 hai6][老師|lou5 si1]。[你都係|Nei5 dou1 hai6][老師|lou5 si1][咩|me1]？
lines.id: No, I'm a teacher. You're a teacher too?
lines.literal: not — am, I — am — teacher. you — also — are — teacher — really.

lines.speaker: 黃麗:
lines.text: [我唔係|Ngo5 m4 hai6][老師|lou5 si1]，[我係|ngo5 hai6][學生|hok6 saang1]。
lines.id: I'm not a teacher, I'm a student.
lines.literal: I — not — am — teacher, I — am — student.

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.text: [你個名|Nei5 go3 meng2][好好聽|hou2 hou2 teng1]。
lines.id: Your name sounds nice.
lines.literal: you — classifier — name — filler — nice — hear.

lines.speaker: 黃麗:
lines.text: [多謝|Do1 ze6]！[聽日見|Ting1 jat6 gin3]！
lines.id: Thank you! See you tomorrow!
lines.literal: many — thanks. tomorrow — see.

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.text: [拜拜|Baai1 baai3]！
lines.id: Bye!
lines.literal: bye — bye.

notes: **[你好|Nei5 hou2] literally means “you good”** — and it's a **statement**, not a question. Use it any time, with anyone, like “hello”. 🇭🇰 Worth knowing: Hongkongers almost never ask each other [你好嗎|nei5 hou2 maa3]？ That's a textbook line. What people really say to friends is [點呀|Dim2 aa3]？ or [食咗飯未呀|Sik6 zo2 faan6 mei6 aa3]？

**[姓|sing3] is only for surnames, [叫|giu3] is for names.** [我姓黃|Ngo5 sing3 Wong4] = my surname is Wong. [我叫黃麗|Ngo5 giu3 Wong4 Lai6] = my name is Wong Lai. ⚠️ Learners with a single name often say 我姓安迪 — which sounds like “my surname is Andi”. When in doubt, just use 叫; it's almost always right.

**Chinese names run in the opposite order from English ones: surname first, then given name.** 黃麗 = surname 黃, given name 麗. Chinese surnames are nearly always one syllable, and in Hong Kong they're romanized by their Cantonese sound — 黃 is *Wong*, not *Huang*; 陳 is *Chan*, not *Chen*; 李 is *Lee*, not *Li*.
**[呢|ne1] bounces a question back without repeating it.** After someone asks you something, just answer and add [你呢|Nei5 ne1]？ It saves a whole sentence and sounds very natural.

**⚠️ The Cantonese word for “not” is [唔|m4], not 不.** If you've studied Mandarin, this is the first habit to break. 唔 is said with closed lips through the nose — just *m*, no vowel at all. [唔係|m4 hai6] = no, isn't; [唔去|m4 heoi3] = not go; [唔知|m4 zi1] = don't know.

**⚠️ [都|dou1] “also” goes before the verb, never at the end of the sentence.** [我都係老師|Ngo5 dou1 hai6 lou5 si1] = I'm a teacher too. The English order “I'm a teacher too” doesn't exist in Cantonese. Note too that Cantonese 都 carries two meanings: “also” and “all”.

**[好|hou2] in [好開心|hou2 hoi1 sam1] doesn't mean “very”.** It's a required filler placed before adjectives: [我開心|ngo5 hoi1 sam1] without 好 sounds unfinished, as if more is coming. 🔁 We'll sort this out fully in Unit 8 — for now, just learn the pair by heart.

grammars.title: 係 — one verb is enough for this whole unit
body: [係|hai6] links two **nouns**: A 係 B means “A is B”. Cantonese verbs never change form, so 係 is exactly the same for I, you, he, we, and they — no *am / is / are* as in English.
To negate it, just put [唔|m4] in front: [唔係|m4 hai6].

head: Person
Cantonese
Example
rows: [我係老師|Ngo5 hai6 lou5 si1]。 I'm a teacher.
[你係學生|Nei5 hai6 hok6 saang1]。 You're a student.
[佢係醫生|Keoi5 hai6 ji1 sang1]。 He/She is a doctor.
[我哋係印尼人|Ngo5 dei6 hai6 Jan3 nei4 jan4]。 We're Indonesian.
[你哋係老師|Nei5 dei6 hai6 lou5 si1]。 You're teachers.
[佢哋係學生|Keoi5 dei6 hai6 hok6 saang1]。 They're students.

after: ⚠️ **Spoken Cantonese doesn't distinguish “he” and “she”.** Both are [佢|keoi5]. Good news: one word to learn instead of two.
⚠️ **Plurals are made with [哋|dei6], and only for people.** [我哋|ngo5 dei6] = we. But there's no 書哋 for “books” — plural things are handled differently (see Unit 2).

🇭🇰 **Cantonese hardly uses the polite form 您.** To a boss, guest, or elder you still say [你|nei5] — politeness moves into other word choices, such as [請問|cing2 man6] before a question or [貴姓|gwai3 sing3] to ask for a surname.

grammars.title: Three ways to ask yes/no questions
body: Cantonese has three ways, and all three are used every day. The most common one — and the safest for you right now — is the first.

head: Method
Form
Example
Nuance
rows: [你係唔係老師|Nei5 hai6 m4 hai6 lou5 si1]？
[你係老師呀|Nei5 hai6 lou5 si1 aa3]？
[你係老師咩|Nei5 hai6 lou5 si1 me1]？

head: Question
Yes answer
No answer
rows: [你係唔係學生|Nei5 hai6 m4 hai6 hok6 saang1]？

after: **Look at how to answer: Cantonese has no stand-alone words for “yes” and “no”.** Instead you **repeat the verb**, with or without 唔. Asked [你去唔去|nei5 heoi3 m4 heoi3]？, you answer [去|heoi3] or [唔去|m4 heoi3] — not “yes” or “no”.
⚠️ **Don't use Mandarin 嗎.** [你係老師嗎|nei5 hai6 lou5 si1 maa3]？ will be understood but instantly marks you as someone who learned from a Mandarin book. In Hong Kong, use A-唔-A or 呀.
⚠️ **[咩|me1] is not a substitute for 呀.** It carries surprise. [你唔去咩|Nei5 m4 heoi3 me1]？ = “Wait, you're not going?” Using it for ordinary questions makes you sound accusing.

dialogs.title: 對話 2 — Introducing a third person
dialogs.intro: A day later, Wong Lai introduces Andi to her friend in the canteen. Notice how a third person is introduced, and how the question word sits where the answer goes.

lines.speaker: 黃麗:
lines.text: [安迪|On1 dik1]，[呢位|ni1 wai2][係|hai6][我朋友|ngo5 pang4 jau5][陳生|Can4 saang1]。
lines.id: Andi, this is my friend, Mr. Chan.
lines.literal: Andi, this — polite-classifier — is — my — friend — Chan — mister.

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.text: [陳生|Can4 saang1]，[你好|nei5 hou2]。[我叫|Ngo5 giu3][安迪|On1 dik1]。
lines.id: Hello, Mr. Chan. My name is Andi.
lines.literal: Chan — mister, you — good. I — be-called — Andi.

lines.speaker: 陳生:
lines.text: [你好|Nei5 hou2]。[請問|Cing2 man6][你係|nei5 hai6][邊度人|bin1 dou6 jan4][呀|aa3]？
lines.id: Hello. May I ask where you're from?
lines.literal: you — good. please — ask — you — are — which — place — person — huh.

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.text: [我係|Ngo5 hai6][印尼人|Jan3 nei4 jan4]，[喺雅加達嚟|hai2 Ngaa5 gaa1 daat6 lei4]。
lines.id: I'm Indonesian, from Jakarta.
lines.literal: I — am — Indonesia — person, at — Jakarta — come.

lines.speaker: 陳生:
lines.text: [你做|Nei5 zou6][邊行|bin1 hong4][㗎|gaa3]？
lines.id: What line of work are you in?
lines.literal: you — do — which — line — emphasis.

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.text: [我係|Ngo5 hai6][老師|lou5 si1]。[陳生|Can4 saang1][你呢|nei5 ne1]？
lines.id: I'm a teacher. And you, Mr. Chan?
lines.literal: I — am — teacher. Chan — mister — you — how-about.

lines.speaker: 陳生:
lines.text: [我係|Ngo5 hai6][工程師|gung1 cing4 si1]。[佢|Keoi5][都係|dou1 hai6][工程師|gung1 cing4 si1]。
lines.id: I'm an engineer. She's an engineer too.
lines.literal: I — am — engineer. she — also — is — engineer.

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.text: [佢係|Keoi5 hai6][邊位|bin1 wai2][呀|aa3]？
lines.id: Who is she?
lines.literal: she — is — which — polite-classifier — huh.

lines.speaker: 陳生:
lines.text: [佢係|Keoi5 hai6][我同事|ngo5 tung4 si6]，[佢姓|keoi5 sing3][李|Lei5]。
lines.id: She's my colleague; her surname is Lee.
lines.literal: she — is — my — colleague, she — be-surnamed — Lee.

lines.speaker: 黃麗:
lines.text: [我哋|Ngo5 dei6][都唔係|dou1 m4 hai6][工程師|gung1 cing4 si1][喎|wo3]！
lines.id: Neither of us is an engineer, you know!
lines.literal: we — all — not — are — engineer — you-know.

lines.speaker: 陳生:
lines.text: [哈哈|Haa1 haa1]，[唔緊要|m4 gan2 jiu3]。[好開心|Hou2 hoi1 sam1][認識你哋|jing6 sik1 nei5 dei6]。
lines.id: Haha, no problem. Nice to meet you both.
lines.literal: ha — ha, not — important. filler — happy — know — you-all.

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.text: [我都係|Ngo5 dou1 hai6]。[再見|Zoi3 gin3]！
lines.id: Me too. See you!
lines.literal: I — also — am. again — see.

notes: **[呢位|ni1 wai2] and [邊位|bin1 wai2] use the polite classifier [位|wai2].** For people who deserve respect — guests, customers, elders — use 位, not 個. [呢個人|ni1 go3 jan4] isn't wrong, but it sounds cold when the person is standing in front of you.

**⚠️ Cantonese question words sit where the answer goes.** [你係邊度人|Nei5 hai6 bin1 dou6 jan4]？ — 邊度 takes exactly the slot the answer will fill (印尼). Cantonese does **not** move question words to the front like English. The word order is the same as the statement.

**[生|saang1] in [陳生|Can4 saang1] is short for [先生|sin1 saang1], “Mr.”.** It goes **after** the surname. Female counterparts: [小姐|siu2 ze2] (Miss) and [太|taai2], short for [太太|taai3 taai2] (Mrs.). So 陳生 = Mr. Chan, [陳太|Can4 taai2] = Mrs. Chan, [陳小姐|Can4 siu2 ze2] = Miss Chan.

**[請問|Cing2 man6] is one word that changes the feel of your whole sentence.** Literally “please ask”, it goes before a question to a stranger. Without it, a grammatically perfect question can sound like an interrogation.
**[喺…嚟|hai2 … lei4] = “come from …”.** [我喺雅加達嚟|Ngo5 hai2 Ngaa5 gaa1 daat6 lei4] = I'm from Jakarta. 🔁 [喺|hai2] is the word you'll use constantly for “at/in”; it's covered fully in Unit 7.

**[㗎|gaa3] at the end of a question stresses that you really want to know.** It's a fusion of 嘅 + 呀. With no particle at all, [你做邊行|nei5 zou6 bin1 hong4]？ sounds abrupt; with 㗎 it sounds natural. 🔁 The whole particle family is gathered in the summary at the back of the book.

**[喎|wo3] marks news you've just realized.** [我哋都唔係工程師喎|Ngo5 dei6 dou1 m4 hai6 gung1 cing4 si1 wo3]！ = “hey, neither of us is an engineer, you know”. This particle makes sentences sound alive, and English has no neat match beyond “you know” or “oh, hey”.

**[都|dou1] in [我哋都唔係|ngo5 dei6 dou1 m4 hai6] means “all”, not “also”.** The subject decides: when it's plural, 都 leans toward “all of them”. [我哋都係印尼人|Ngo5 dei6 dou1 hai6 Jan3 nei4 jan4] = we're all Indonesian.

grammars.title: Question words: they sit where the answer goes
body: This is the biggest effort-saver in all of Cantonese. Build the statement first, then **replace the part you don't know** with the question word. The word order doesn't change at all.

head: Question word
Jyutping
Meaning
Example
rows: [佢係邊個|Keoi5 hai6 bin1 go3]？ Who is he?
[你搵邊位|Nei5 wan2 bin1 wai2]？ Who are you looking for?
[呢個係乜嘢|Ni1 go3 hai6 mat1 je5]？ What is this?
[你喺邊度|Nei5 hai2 bin1 dou6]？ Where are you?
[你幾時嚟|Nei5 gei2 si4 lei4]？ When are you coming?
[點解唔去|Dim2 gaai2 m4 heoi3]？ Why not go?
[點樣去|Dim2 joeng2 heoi3]？ How do you get there?
[幾多錢|Gei2 do1 cin2]？ How much is it?

head: Statement
As a question
rows: [佢係老師|Keoi5 hai6 lou5 si1]。 He's a teacher.
[佢係邊個|Keoi5 hai6 bin1 go3]？ Who is he?
[我去旺角|Ngo5 heoi3 Wong6 gok3]。 I'm going to Mongkok.
[你去邊度|Nei5 heoi3 bin1 dou6]？ Where are you going?
[我食飯|Ngo5 sik6 faan6]。 I'm eating rice.
[你食乜嘢|Nei5 sik6 mat1 je5]？ What are you eating?

after: 🇭🇰 **[乜嘢|mat1 je5] is often shortened to [咩|me1] in fast speech.** [你叫咩名|Nei5 giu3 me1 meng2]？ = what's your name — this is the form you'll actually hear on the street. Don't confuse it with the surprise particle 咩 at the end of a sentence; this one sits in the middle, before a noun.

⚠️ **Questions with a question word don't need 呀 if you mean them neutrally… but you can add it to soften them.** [你去邊度呀|Nei5 heoi3 bin1 dou6 aa3]？ sounds friendlier than without 呀. What's wrong is adding 咩 — that turns it into an accusation.

**There are two levels for asking someone's name.** To a peer: [你叫咩名呀|Nei5 giu3 me1 meng2 aa3]？ To someone you should respect: [請問你貴姓呀|Cing2 man6 nei5 gwai3 sing3 aa3]？ — literally “what is your honorable surname”, answered with just the surname: [我姓黃|Ngo5 sing3 Wong4]。

blocks.text: 你好 is always correct, but Hongkongers rarely use it between people who already know each other. The phrases below make your greetings sound natural, not like a textbook.

head: Greeting
When to use it
Natural reply
rows: Any time, especially with new people
Morning, until about eleven. Very common at the office and in the elevator
To a group of people at once
“How's it going?” to friends — far more common than 你好嗎
[食咗飯未呀|Sik6 zo2 faan6 mei6 aa3]？
Friendly greeting, literally “eaten yet?” — not an invitation to eat
In every textbook, rarely said by Hongkongers. Safe but stiff

head: Saying goodbye
Nuance
rows: The most common, any situation. From “bye bye”
A bit more formal, fine anywhere
Said by the **host** to a departing guest — literally “walk slowly”
“Let's have tea sometime” — a parting pleasantry, rarely actually scheduled

blocks.title: Manners to know from day one
items: **[唔該|M4 goi1]** — the most useful word in all of Hong Kong. It means “thank you” for a **service** (a waiter bringing tea, someone holding the elevator), and also “excuse me” to call a waiter, and “please” when asking for something.

**[多謝|Do1 ze6]** — “thank you” for **things**: gifts, souvenirs, money, compliments. ⚠️ The difference between 唔該 and 多謝 is real and instantly noticeable. When a waiter brings food, say 唔該; when a friend gives you a present, say 多謝. The reply to both: [唔使客氣|M4 sai2 haak3 hei3]。
**[對唔住|Deoi3 m4 zyu6]** — sorry, for a real mistake. The reply is [唔緊要|M4 gan2 jiu3] or [冇所謂|Mou5 so2 wai6].
**[唔好意思|M4 hou2 ji3 si1]** — “oops, sorry” for small things: cutting in, being five minutes late, bothering someone. Used far more often than 對唔住.
**[唔該借借|M4 goi1 ze3 ze3]** — “excuse me, coming through”. The phrase that will save you every day on the MTR at rush hour.

blocks.text: Saying where you're from in Cantonese follows one pattern that never changes: **place name + 人**. No linking word, no change of form.

head: Country / city
Jyutping
Person
rows: [馬來西亞人|maa5 loi4 sai1 aa3 jan4]

blocks.text: Saying your job uses 係, exactly like saying where you're from. There's no article like English *a*: [我係老師|Ngo5 hai6 lou5 si1], not “I am a teacher” word for word.

blocks.title: Asking about jobs: three forms people really use
items: [你做邊行㗎|Nei5 zou6 bin1 hong4 gaa3]？ — “What line of work are you in?” The most natural among adults.
[你做乜嘢工㗎|Nei5 zou6 mat1 je5 gung1 gaa3]？ — “What do you do for work?” A bit more casual.
[你係咪學生呀|Nei5 hai6 mai6 hok6 saang1 aa3]？ — 🇭🇰 [係咪|hai6 mai6] is the fast form of 係唔係, and it's what you'll actually hear most. Use either freely; both are correct.
